raw_case_text:
The case is a 32-year-old female patient with a history of cadaveric donor RT in 2006 due to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. She received induction therapy with basiliximab and maintenance therapy with tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and deflazacort. She consulted for a 4-week history of diarrheal stools 4 times a day that she controlled with loperamide. In the last week, it was associated with nausea, crampy abdominal pain, and fever. In the last 6 months, she had lost 10 kg and was being managed with oral iron due to normochromic normocytic anemia, with no improvement in hemoglobin levels. She had no other relevant background.
On physical examination, she was tachycardic, afebrile, and normotensive, with abdominal pain in the left flank without signs of peritoneal irritation. Chronic diarrhea and febrile syndrome were considered in an immunosuppressed patient, so studies with fecal microscopy, fecal culture, viral load for CMV, and blood culture were started (Table 1). Due to chronic anemia, studies with folic acid, vitamin B12, ferrokinetic profile, and nutritional profile were extended, confirming iron deficiency anemia.
Renal function was stable with serum creatinine within the patient's usual range. Electrolytes were unaltered, fecal microscopy examination was inflammatory, and cultures were negative. Colonoscopy showed left and transverse colitis with 80% stenosis of the colonic lumen (Figure 1). Biopsies of the compromised segments were taken.
Given the results found in colonoscopy, studies with gastrointestinal film array, CMV viral load in plasma, HIV, and rapid plasma reagin were evaluated, which were negative, as was the Histoplasma urine antigen. Herpes simplex type I and II studies performed in biopsy were negative. Given the suspicion of neoplasia, contrast abdominal tomography was carried out, which showed thickening and enhancement of the walls of the cecum, ascending colon, and hepatic flexure of the colon, with a 4-cm segment with 80% stenosis of the ascending colon lumen. Colon biopsy reported ulcerative component, without identifying microorganisms, dysplasia, or malignancy. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for TB and CMV was positive in the biopsy.
The patient was presented at a meeting considering intestinal Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MT) and CMV coinfection. Treatment with valganciclovir for 4 weeks was decided to manage CMV and 4-drug therapy with isoniazid (INH), rifampin (R), pyrazinamide (Z), ethambutol (E), and pyridoxine for GITB management. Tacrolimus dose was adjusted due to drug interaction with rifampin.
During treatment, elevated transaminases (aspartate aminotransferase 414 U/L and alanine transaminase 990 U/L) and uric acid (16 mg/dL) developed. Hepatotoxicity associated with INH was considered, so it was assessed by the pulmonologist who changed INH to moxifloxacin, with improvement in the liver profile. Moxifloxacin, R, and Z were continued for 9 months. The evolution was satisfactory, with the resolution of diarrhea, improvement in anemia, stable renal function (1.48 mg/dL), and weight recovery.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old female renal transplant recipient presented with a 4-week history of watery diarrhea (4 times daily) and a 1-week history of nausea, crampy left flank/abdominal pain, and fever, on a background of a 10-kg weight loss over 6 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had undergone deceased-donor renal transplantation in 2006 for membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and deflazacort) and had lost 10 kg over the preceding 6 months with refractory normocytic iron-deficiency anemia. She presented with 4 weeks of diarrhea partially controlled with loperamide, complicated over the final week by nausea, crampy abdominal pain, and fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease secondary to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis status post cadaveric renal transplant in 2006, and chronic iron-deficiency anemia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic diarrhea, nausea, crampy abdominal pain, fever, and 10-kg weight loss over 6 months. Home medications: tacrolimus, mycophenolate, deflazacort, oral iron, and loperamide.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: tachycardic, afebrile, and normotensive. Abdomen: tenderness in the left flank without peritoneal irritation.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs: normochromic normocytic iron-deficiency anemia (normal folate and vitamin B12), stable baseline serum creatinine, normal electrolytes, inflammatory fecal microscopy, and negative stool, blood, and GI FilmArray panel tests; negative plasma CMV viral load, HIV, RPR, and urine Histoplasma antigen.
objective.advanced_workup: Colonoscopy: left and transverse colitis with an 80% luminal stenosis. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT: wall thickening and enhancement of the cecum, ascending colon, and hepatic flexure with a 4-cm segment of 80% luminal stenosis in the ascending colon. Colonic mucosal biopsy & PCR: ulcerative colitis without visible microorganisms, dysplasia, or malignancy on routine histology; negative HSV-1/2 PCR, but positive tissue PCR for both Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Cytomegalovirus (CMV).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Stenosing intestinal Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Cytomegalovirus (CMV) coinfection in a renal transplant recipient (gastrointestinal histoplasmosis and colonic malignancy ruled out). Confirmation: Positive tissue PCR for both Mycobacterium tuberculosis and CMV on stenotic colonic mucosal biopsies, with negative urine Histoplasma antigen. Plan & clinical course: Treated with a 4-week course of oral valganciclovir for CMV and a 9-month anti-tuberculosis regimen (initiated on isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol; isoniazid switched to moxifloxacin due to transaminitis [AST 414 U/L, ALT 990 U/L] and hyperuricemia [16 mg/dL]), achieving complete resolution of diarrhea, weight recovery, improved anemia, and stable allograft function (creatinine 1.48 mg/dL).
